extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof and logic techniques (introductory proof course)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing clear, correct proofs in introductory undergraduate mathematics, covering direct proof, contrapositive, proof by cases, logical equivalences, divisibility, congruence, and modular arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn your reader when using contrapositive
rubrics_metrics.description: As noted in the example above, when you prove the contrapositive of the result you should warn the reader of what you are going to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief explicit phrases such as “We prove the contrapositive…”, “Consider the contrapositive…”, or even “Do contrapositive…”. A few words can save the reader confusion about why you are assuming the conclusion is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer contrapositive when easier
rubrics_metrics.description: (P ⇒ Q) ≡ (¬Q ⇒ ¬P); consider proving the contrapositive if the direct approach is stuck or awkward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the contrapositive in scratchwork to assess if it simplifies the argument (e.g., parity proofs often become straightforward when contraposed). If it is easier, explicitly state you are proving the contrapositive and proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical equivalences and know common identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard logical equivalences (Implication, Contrapositive, Biconditional, Double negation, Commutative, Associative, Distributive, DeMorgan’s laws) to rewrite statements into easier-to-prove forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 4.2.3 lists these: (P ⇒ Q) ≡ (¬P ∨ Q), (P ⇒ Q) ≡ (¬Q ⇒ ¬P), (P ⇔ Q) ≡ ((P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ P)), ¬(¬P) ≡ P, commutativity and associativity of ∧/∨, distributive laws, and DeMorgan’s laws. Chain them to transform statements rather than forcing a direct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negate statements carefully (including inequalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the logical equivalences and DeMorgan’s laws to negate compound statements correctly; remember specific inequality negations (negation of a < b is a ≥ b, negation of a ≤ b is a > b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply results like ∼(P ⇒ Q) ≡ P ∧ (∼Q) and ∼(P ⇔ Q) ≡ (P ∧ ∼Q) ∨ (Q ∧ ∼P). When negating inequalities be careful: e.g., ∼(x < 1) is x ≥ 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove biconditionals by proving both implications
rubrics_metrics.description: To show P ⇔ Q, rewrite as (P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ P) and prove each direction separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the plan (e.g., “We first prove P ⇒ Q, then Q ⇒ P”), then present the two sub-proofs clearly. Each implication may use different techniques (direct, contrapositive, cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure proof-by-cases explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: When the hypothesis is a disjunction or you can partition possibilities (e.g., parity, remainders), break the proof into N cases and prove each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that the hypothesis breaks into cases, label each case (Case 1, Case 2, ...), prove each, and summarize at the end that all cases were handled. Follow Lemma 4.2.8 ((P ∨ R) ⇒ Q) ≡ ((P ⇒ Q) ∧ (R ⇒ Q)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure you have found and covered all cases; be cautious with 'WLOG'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not omit cases unless symmetry or a valid argument justifies it; 'WLOG' can be dangerous and lead to mistakes if not fully justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inexperienced writers, perform all cases in scratchwork first. Only omit a case in the write-up if you explicitly justify why it is symmetric or equivalent to another case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about domain assumptions and use them
rubrics_metrics.description: State domain assumptions (e.g., 'Let n ∈ Z') since integerness or positiveness can simplify logical equivalences and case splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use domain facts like 'every integer is either even or odd' to transform hypotheses into useful disjunctions for case analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions directly for divisibility and related properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving divisibility statements use the definition (a | b means b = ka for some k ∈ Z) to substitute and conclude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the definition to introduce integer multipliers, then manipulate algebraically; for contrapositive handling, re-express 'not divisible' via Euclidean division or remainders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Euclidean division / uniqueness when working with remainders
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition integers by their remainders modulo n (e.g., n = 3k, 3k+1, 3k+2) and use uniqueness of Euclidean division to rule out divisibility possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially useful for proofs about divisibility by small moduli (e.g., showing 3 | n ⇔ 3 | n^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use congruence modulo n and modular arithmetic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace repetitive remainder-case analysis by congruence notation: a ≡ b (mod n) when n | (a − b). Use modular arithmetic properties (addition, subtraction, multiplication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 5.3.3: if a ≡ c (mod n) and b ≡ d (mod n) then a±b ≡ c±d (mod n) and ab ≡ cd (mod n). Congruence streamlines parity and divisibility proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sloppy or hand-wavy language
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious with phrases like 'Clearly', 'Obviously', 'It is easy to show', or prematurely omitted details; these can hide errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such phrases can conceal gaps; prefer brief explicit justification or a reference to an earlier, obvious fact. Keep a list of dangerous shorthand phrases and avoid them in formal write-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish scratchwork from final write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to be a bit sloppy in scratchwork, but the final written proof should be tidy, explicit about assumptions, and may omit tedious algebra without skipping logical justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the final proof remove routine algebraic manipulations for readability, but do not omit essential logical steps. State technique choices (contrapositive, cases) so the reader follows the structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label proof techniques when used
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader which method you are using (direct proof, contrapositive, proof by cases, contradiction) to clarify structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'We prove the contrapositive' or 'We proceed by cases' prepare the reader and avoid confusion about assumed statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for illegal algebraic steps in faulty proofs (e.g., dividing by zero, hidden assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing purported proofs, look for invalid operations like cancelling a factor that may be zero, reusing the same symbol for different meanings, or assuming what you need to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common faulty-proof patterns include cancelling (x−y) when x=y, or reusing the same constant k for distinct divisibility steps. Identify and explain these issues before providing a correct proof.
